body:
> Worse, https://jsfiddle.net/n04m3jpo/ shows a variant with promise handlers (instead of setTimeout's Web IDL callbacks) where Chrome and Safari do run the promise handler, and Firefox does not.

That both Chrome and Safari run the promise handlers here give me pause that changing the behavior might not be web compatible. What's your intuition?

I agree it's not clear-cut. It's a combination of:

- Firefox gets away with it.

- Chrome and Safari don't run Web IDL handlers, which are potentially more common.

- Anything involving detached frames is a mess and unlikely to be something web developers can rely on. E.g. inside your callback the properties of the global object will mostly be nulled out or throw exceptions, in inconsistent ways across browsers.

I think the main risk would be if there's a site which is trying to do "JS-spec-only" things (e.g. Node.js-isomorphic code) on detached iframes, and using promises to schedule things there. But such a site wouldn't work in Firefox, so I'm hoping such cases are rare...

Separately from my intuition on whether this is compatible, I also think it's desirable, as part of the ongoing efforts of folks like @xharaken and his team to make detached iframes as GC-able as possible.

I used Claude to help write tentative tests in web-platform-tests/wpt#63315:

> The tests call a callback from an iframe that's been removed or navigated away, and cover invoke, construct, call a user object's operation, and promise jobs. The Web IDL callbacks tested are timers, queueMicrotask, rAF, MutationObserver, event handlers and listeners, custom element constructors and connectedCallback, ReadableStream start, NodeFilter, and XPathNSResolver.
> 
> Current behavior:
> 
> |                                | Chrome Canary                           | Firefox Nightly | Safari TP                                         |
> |--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-----------------|---------------------------------------------------|
> | Web IDL callbacks              | not called, except ReadableStream start | not called      | called                                            |
> | Promise jobs, iframe removed   | run                                     | run             | run, except for the iframe's own promise or await |
> | Promise jobs, iframe navigated | don't run                               | don't run       | run                                               |
> 
> So Firefox now matches Chrome for the setTimeout example in the OP, and for promise reactions when the iframe is removed. When Chrome and Firefox don't call a callback from a synchronous API, they seem to throw instead, e.g. createElement() for a custom element constructor.
> 
> The tests expect what Chrome and Firefox mostly do: Web IDL callbacks aren't called, and promise jobs run if the iframe is removed but not if it's navigated. The removed/navigated difference for promise jobs seems odd, though.

FYI: After https://github.com/LadybirdBrowser/ladybird/pull/12697 is merged, Ladybird will be doing what Chrome and Firefox do; that is, Ladybird will refuse a callback whose realm’s global object is a `Window` whose associated `Document` isn’t fully active (and throw a `NotSupportedError`) when invoking a callback function, constructing one, and calling a user object’s operation.

Against the tentative tests in https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/63315, that takes Ladybird from 7/25 to 25/25 in `invoke.tentative.html`, from 3/9 to 9/9 in `construct.tentative.html`, and from 10/25 to 23/25 in `call-user-object-operation.tentative.html`.

The other 2 tests out of the 25 in `call-user-object-operation.tentative.html` are the `XPathNSResolver` cases in the fully active state, where Ladybird doesn’t call the resolver at all yet.

Promise jobs are unchanged: Like Safari, Ladybird still runs them for a navigated-away iframe, so 4 of the 13 subtests in `promise-jobs.tentative.html` fail.
